title: Earth Materials and the Rock Cycle

short_title: minerals, rocks, the rock cycle and resources
standard_text: Earth materials are changed as they cycle through the geosphere and are used as resources: minerals, igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks, the rock cycle, and earth resources. (summary of BC's Curriculum, Earth Sciences 11)
meta_desc: Free Earth Sciences 11 worksheets (BC Curriculum): minerals, rocks, the rock cycle and resources. 100 questions with answers.
key_big: Rocks change type through the rock cycle.
key_sub: Minerals are identified by hardness, streak, lustre and cleavage.
body_html:
How to think about it

A mineral is a naturally occurring inorganic solid with a definite chemical composition and crystal structure. Minerals are identified by colour, streak, lustre, hardness (Mohs scale), cleavage and fracture.

Igneous rock forms from cooled magma (intrusive, coarse crystals) or lava (extrusive, fine crystals). Sedimentary rock forms from compacted and cemented sediment. Metamorphic rock forms by heat and pressure. BC mines copper, gold, coal and gravel; resource use must be balanced with protecting land and water.

Example

Granite has large crystals. Did it cool quickly or slowly?

Large crystals need time.

Answer: slowly, underground

Example

Shale is heated and squeezed into slate. What type of rock is slate?

Changed by heat and pressure

Answer: metamorphic

Common mistakes

  • Thinking colour is the most reliable way to identify a mineral.
  • Thinking rocks follow only one path in the rock cycle.
  • Mixing up minerals and rocks.

items.q: What is the principle of superposition?
c: in undisturbed sedimentary layers, the lowest layers are the oldest
all layers formed at the same time
the youngest layers are at the bottom
items.e: It gives relative ages.

items.q: How did the rock of the Organ Pipes in Victoria form?
c: from lava that cooled slowly and cracked into columns
from mudstone changed by heat and pressure
from magma that cooled slowly deep underground
from sand and gravel eroded from ancient mountains, then pressed and cemented
items.e: The Organ Pipes in Victoria is basalt (igneous).

items.q: What do 4.4-billion-year-old zircons tell us about early Earth?
c: Earth had no crust for 2 billion years
there was continental crust and probably liquid water very early
items.e: Their oxygen isotopes suggest they formed with water present.

items.q: Which statement about the age of oceanic crust is correct?
c: it is older than most continental crust
it is oldest at mid-ocean ridges
it is the same age everywhere
it is youngest at mid-ocean ridges and gets older away from them
items.e: Oceanic crust is rarely older than about 200 million years.

items.q: What forms where an oceanic plate subducts beneath another plate?
c: a deep trench and a chain of volcanoes
items.e: The Pacific 'Ring of Fire' has many subduction zones.

items.q: Which happened first: the Moon forms after a giant impact, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: They happened at the same time.
the Moon forms after a giant impact
items.e: The Moon forms after a giant impact: about 4.5 billion years ago; the oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: the first animals appear, or the oldest zircon crystals form?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: The oldest zircon crystals form: about 4.4 billion years ago; the first animals appear: about 0.6 billion years ago.

items.q: Which happened first: Earth forms, or the first microbial fossils (stromatolites)?
c: They happened at the same time.
items.e: Earth forms: about 4.56 billion years ago; the first microbial fossils (stromatolites): about 3.5 billion years ago.

items.q: A sample starts with 160 g of a radioactive parent. How much parent is left after 5 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 5 times: 5 g.

items.q: A sample had 80 g of parent and now has 2.5 g. How many half-lives have passed?
items.e: 80 → 2.5 takes 5 halvings.

items.q: A sample starts with 32 g of a radioactive parent. How much parent is left after 5 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 5 times: 1 g.

items.q: A rock started with 320 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 4 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 320 − 20 = 300 g.

items.q: A piece of old wood has 1/64 of its original carbon-14 left (half-life 5730 years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/64 = 6 half-lives; 6 × 5730 = 34380 years.

items.q: A piece of old wood has 1/32 of its original carbon-14 left (half-life 5730 years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/32 = 5 half-lives; 5 × 5730 = 28650 years.

items.q: A mineral has 1/16 of its original uranium-235 left (half-life 704 million years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/16 = 4 half-lives; 4 × 704 = 2816 million years.

items.q: A mineral has 1/8 of its original uranium-235 left (half-life 704 million years). How old is it?
items.e: 1/8 = 3 half-lives; 3 × 704 = 2112 million years.

items.q: A volcano releases sulfur dioxide that cools the climate. Which spheres interact?
c: the biosphere and the hydrosphere only
items.e: Volcanic gases enter the atmosphere.

items.q: A sample starts with 160 g of a radioactive parent. How much parent is left after 2 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 2 times: 40 g.

items.q: A sample starts with 16 g of a radioactive parent. How much parent is left after 3 half-lives?
items.e: Halve 3 times: 2 g.

items.q: What is a reservoir (store) in an Earth system model?
c: a place where matter is held for a time, such as the ocean or the atmosphere
items.e: Fluxes move matter between reservoirs.

items.q: Which type of plate boundary is the Alpine Fault in New Zealand, where plates slide past each other?
items.e: Transform boundaries cause large earthquakes.

items.q: A rock started with 160 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 3 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 160 − 20 = 140 g.

items.q: A rock has uranium-235 and lead-207 in a ratio of 1 : 63 (half-life of uranium-235: 704 million years). How old is it? (Assume all the lead-207 came from decay.)
items.e: 1 : 63 means 1/64 is left → 6 half-lives = 4224 million years.

items.q: A sample had 128 g of parent and now has 8 g. How many half-lives have passed?
items.e: 128 → 8 takes 4 halvings.

items.q: A rock started with 80 g of parent isotope and no daughter. After 4 half-lives, how much daughter isotope is there?
items.e: Daughter = original − parent left = 80 − 5 = 75 g.

items.q: Rain falling on a mountain wears away rock and carries sediment to the sea. Which spheres interact?
items.e: Weathering and erosion link the spheres.

items.q: How do we know the outer core is liquid?
c: S-waves (shear waves) do not travel through it, leaving an S-wave shadow zone
items.e: P-waves pass through but are refracted.

items.q: A sample had 160 g of parent and now has 40 g. How many half-lives have passed?
items.e: 160 → 40 takes 2 halvings.
